subject: How to specify nested random effects?

messages.author: ad1119992218e9cb
messages.subject: How to specify nested random effects?
parts:
I have count data from multiple sites (e.g. S1, S2, S3, S4) which are located in two areas ("north", "south"), with a pile of continuous covariates, and multiple years (modelled with "rw2").

How would I specify the model to indicate that sites 1 & 2 are always in "north" area and sites 3 & 4 are always in "south" area ?

I've tried the following specifications (leaving out model = "iid" from each term for clarity):

f1 = count ~ f(area) + f(site) + cov
f2 = count ~ f(area, site) + cov
f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(area2, site) + cov  # area2 being a duplicate of area 
f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(site, area2) + cov

In lme4 I'd specify: count ~ cov + (1 | area / site)

Which, if any, is the correct INLA specification? 

(Please excuse the basic question--I'm brand new to R-INLA, but enjoying it so far!)

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
parts:
Hi,

it depends on what precisely the "nested" aspect should mean; someone
with familiarity of lme4 might have a clearer answer to this,
but my understanding is that "(1 | area / site)" is equivalent to "(1
| area) + (1 | area:site)". However, the interaction term "area:site"
seems to me to be equivalent to just "site", since each site can only
be located within one of your two areas. That would indicate that
f(area) + f(site) is what you need.

An exception to that would be if the lme4 "(1 | area:site)" implies
that each area should have its own variance parameter for the
area:site effect. If that's the case, I believe you would need
to split the site index vector into site1 and site2; if
area = c(1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2)
and
site <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)
let
site1 <- site2 <- site
site1[area != 1] <- NA # site1: c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, NA, NA)
site2[area != 2] <- NA # site1: c(NA, NA, 3, NA, 5, 6, 7)
and use
f(area) + f(site1, n = 7) + f(site2, n = 7)
in the formula, so that each area gets it's own iid-precision
parameter for the site effects.

For a smaller computational model the site indices within site1 and
site2 should be compressed into
site1: c(1, 2, NA, 3, NA, NA, NA)
site2: c(NA, NA, 1, NA, 2, 3, 4)
and the "n" parameters to f can be removed.

If there are no repeated measurements, this is easily done:
site1 <- site2 <- site
site1[area != 1] <- NA
site2[area != 2] <- NA
site1[area == 1] <- seq_len(sum(area == 1))
site2[area == 2] <- seq_len(sum(area == 2))

If there _are_ repeated measurements, more care needs to be taken when
renumbering the sites, so that all observations for a site is mapped
to the same new index.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
parts:
Hi Finn,

I have a question about the nested effects. Say I want to get the non-linear effect of covariate x for each season in two different cities, i.e. "x | city / season". 

Right now, I create a new index: 1 = season 1 in city 1, 2 = season 2 in city 1, 3 = season 3 in city 1, 4 = season 4 in city 1,  5 = season 1 in city 2, 6 = season 2 in city 2, 7 = season 3 in city 2, 8 = season 4 in city 2.

I write the formula as: 
form <- y ~ 0 + f(x, replicate=index, model='rw1') 

So I am taking the eight groups (4 seasons * 2 cities) totally separately, but how can I specify that group 1-4 belong to city 1, group 5-8 belong to city 2?

Thank you in advance!

Rujia

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
parts:
Ok, so the maths doesn't indicate that you want the random effect
variance \sigma^2 to be diffrent for each city, but your text does say
that.
I think Haavard commented on this in another list email recently. The
basic approach would be to have one f() per city, since that would
give you different sigma for each city.
But that can easily be a lot of variance parameters with many cities,
so I woulnd't recommend that unless the number of cities is small (2-4
perhaps, but that's depending on problem size)

Finn

>> >
>> > On Sunday, March 17, 2019 at 9:19:37 PM UTC-4, Finn Lindgren wrote:
>> >>
>> >> Hi,
>> >>
>> >> it depends on what precisely the "nested" aspect should mean; someone
>> >> with familiarity of lme4 might have a clearer answer to this,
>> >> but my understanding is that "(1 | area / site)" is equivalent to "(1
>> >> | area) + (1 | area:site)". However, the interaction term "area:site"
>> >> seems to me to be equivalent to just "site", since each site can only
>> >> be located within one of your two areas. That would indicate that
>> >> f(area) + f(site) is what you need.
>> >>
>> >> An exception to that would be if the lme4 "(1 | area:site)" implies
>> >> that each area should have its own variance parameter for the
>> >> area:site effect. If that's the case, I believe you would need
>> >> to split the site index vector into site1 and site2; if
>> >> area = c(1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2)
>> >> and
>> >> site <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)
>> >> let
>> >> site1 <- site2 <- site
>> >> site1[area != 1] <- NA # site1: c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, NA, NA)
>> >> site2[area != 2] <- NA # site1: c(NA, NA, 3, NA, 5, 6, 7)
>> >> and use
>> >> f(area) + f(site1, n = 7) + f(site2, n = 7)
>> >> in the formula, so that each area gets it's own iid-precision
>> >> parameter for the site effects.
>> >>
>> >> For a smaller computational model the site indices within site1 and
>> >> site2 should be compressed into
>> >> site1: c(1, 2, NA, 3, NA, NA, NA)
>> >> site2: c(NA, NA, 1, NA, 2, 3, 4)
>> >> and the "n" parameters to f can be removed.
>> >>
>> >> If there are no repeated measurements, this is easily done:
>> >> site1 <- site2 <- site
>> >> site1[area != 1] <- NA
>> >> site2[area != 2] <- NA
>> >> site1[area == 1] <- seq_len(sum(area == 1))
>> >> site2[area == 2] <- seq_len(sum(area == 2))
>> >>
>> >> If there _are_ repeated measurements, more care needs to be taken when
>> >> renumbering the sites, so that all observations for a site is mapped
>> >> to the same new index.
>> >>
>> >> Finn
>> >>
>> >> On Mon, 18 Mar 2019 at 00:20, <attn...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >> >
>> >> > I have count data from multiple sites (e.g. S1, S2, S3, S4) which are located in two areas ("north", "south"), with a pile of continuous covariates, and multiple years (modelled with "rw2").
>> >> >
>> >> > How would I specify the model to indicate that sites 1 & 2 are always in "north" area and sites 3 & 4 are always in "south" area ?
>> >> >
>> >> > I've tried the following specifications (leaving out model = "iid" from each term for clarity):
>> >> >
>> >> > f1 = count ~ f(area) + f(site) + cov
>> >> > f2 = count ~ f(area, site) + cov
>> >> > f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(area2, site) + cov # area2 being a duplicate of area
>> >> > f3 = count ~ f(area) + f(site, area2) + cov
>> >> >
>> >> > In lme4 I'd specify: count ~ cov + (1 | area / site)
>> >> >
>> >> > Which, if any, is the correct INLA specification?
>> >> >
>> >> > (Please excuse the basic question--I'm brand new to R-INLA, but enjoying it so far!)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
parts:
Hi Finn,

I searched the forum, but found nothing on it. To have one f() for each city, do you mean something like joint model? For each city, I need to create a stack? If my model is a hurdle model with a probability sub-model and a positive sub-model, and there are 4 cities, should I have eight stacks?

Thanks,
Rujia

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
parts:
I just mean that for city 1 you set c(1,2,3,NA,NA,NA) and for city 2 c(NA,NA,NA,1,2,3) and use those for defining separate f() models if the first three observations come from city 1 and and the last three from city 2. NA there means “no contribution from this model component”.

I haven’t done hurdle models, sorry, but you’d likely just need one stack per likelihood (so 2, I guess), if you follow the technique above within each of them.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify nested random effects?
parts:
Hi,

In addition to what others have said, in the book by Wang et al. (page 120) they describe how to fit near mixed models using the 'lmer' function to define the matrices of fixed and random effects and INLA latent effect 'z'. You may also find this interesting:

https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-multilevel.html

Here, 'model.matrix' is used to define the matrices of random effects, which requires a formula and a data.frame and simplifies the model definition.

Best,

Virgilio
